items.title: Billy Mitchell interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, November 16, 1995
items.q: we had a sextet for a small time a couple of years, Dave Burns, Bobby Hutcherson, Herman Wright, Candy Finch and Al and myself.

ctx.x: You did some playing with Al Grey after the Basie band, is that right?

Yeah, we had a small group together. I first met Al way back in that Lucky Millinder band in ‘48. And then after we had both left Basie’s band we had a sextet for a small time a couple of years, Dave Burns, Bobby Hutcherson, Herman Wright, Candy Finch and Al and myself.
Who would handle the business for a group like that?

items.title: Bobby Hutcherson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I got with Billy and Al. We play two weeks opposite Mingus.

ctx.x: Do you remember how old you were about this time?

I’ll say 9. So Eric started doing all this different stuff. He was into doing so much stuff and moving. He wanted to go to New York. So my sister started going out with Billy Mitchell from Count Basie’s band. Billy comes over to the house. Right when that happened, I was – I had been – it was summertime, and I was walking down the street. I came past this guy. His name was Percy Smalley. He had an outdoor speaker. He’s playing the Giants of Jazz. He’s playing Bemsha Swing. I’m walking down the street, and as I…

So I saved enough money. I went over – my mom and I went over to this music store in L.A., [?Lockey] Music Company, bought this little funky set of vibes that had the most beautiful little sound. I didn’t realize that the notes were made out of nickel and steel. They don’t make nickel and steel notes any more. When you hit it, it sounded like John Henry hitting the steel-driving thing. PING! You hit the note like this. Beautiful sound. The notes are made out of aluminum now. Beautiful sound.
